stem: In which year did the United Nations come into existence?

options.rationale: Correct: the Charter came into force on 24 October 1945.
This is the year of the Paris Peace Conference and the League.
This is the year in which the Second World War began.
This is the year of the declaration on decolonisation.

explanation: The UN Charter was signed on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October 1945.

stem: Which UN organ has primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security?

options.content: The Security Council
options.rationale: Correct: its decisions are binding on members.

options.content: The General Assembly
options.rationale: The Assembly debates and recommends.

options.content: The Economic and Social Council
options.rationale: ECOSOC co-ordinates economic and social work.

options.content: The International Court of Justice
options.rationale: The Court settles legal disputes between states.

explanation: The Security Council has primary responsibility for peace and security, and its decisions bind members.

stem: Which of these states is a permanent member of the Security Council with the power of veto?

options.content: Germany
options.rationale: Germany is not a permanent member.

options.content: Zimbabwe
options.rationale: Zimbabwe has served as an elected member.

options.content: France
options.rationale: Correct: the permanent members are the USA, Russia, China, France and the UK.

options.content: Brazil
options.rationale: Brazil has served as an elected member only.

explanation: The five permanent members are the United States, Russia (successor to the USSR), China, France and the United Kingdom.

stem: What is the veto in the Security Council?

options.content: The power of the General Assembly to dismiss any member of the Council
options.rationale: The Assembly has no such power.

options.content: The right of the Secretary-General to cancel any resolution after it is passed
options.rationale: The Secretary-General has no such right.

options.content: The power of a permanent member to block a decision by voting against it
options.rationale: Correct: one negative vote from a permanent member stops it.

options.content: The duty of every member to provide troops whenever the Council asks
options.rationale: The veto is a power to block, not a duty.

explanation: A negative vote by any of the five permanent members blocks a substantive decision of the Council.

stem: What did Security Council Resolution 232 of December 1966 do?

options.content: Admitted Zimbabwe to the United Nations as a new member
options.rationale: Zimbabwe joined in 1980.

options.content: Sent peacekeepers to supervise the independence of Namibia
options.rationale: That happened in 1989-90.

options.content: Created the World Health Organization as a specialised agency
options.rationale: WHO was created in 1948.

options.content: Imposed sanctions on Rhodesia after UDI
options.rationale: Correct: the first mandatory sanctions in UN history.

explanation: Resolution 232 imposed mandatory selective sanctions on Rhodesia; Resolution 253 in 1968 extended them.
hints: It was a response to UDI of 1965.

stem: Why did the founders of the UN include the United States and the Soviet Union and give the Security Council power to act?

options.content: To make sure the General Assembly would have no part in any decisions at all
options.rationale: The Assembly remained a major organ.

options.content: To prevent smaller states from ever joining the organisation in later years
options.rationale: Membership was open to peace-loving states.

options.content: To give the United Nations its own standing army from the very first day
options.rationale: The UN has no standing army.

options.content: To correct League weaknesses, such as missing great powers and no enforcement
options.rationale: Correct: the founders learned from the League.

explanation: The League lacked the United States and had no real power to enforce decisions; the UN was designed to include the great powers and give the Council the ability to act.

stem: Which criticism of the UN is best supported by the work of the Security Council?

options.content: The Council has no power to make any decision that binds a state
options.rationale: Its decisions are binding.

options.content: The veto can prevent action when permanent members disagree
options.rationale: Correct: this limited the Council in the Cold War.

options.content: All members of the UN have a veto in the Security Council
options.rationale: Only five have it.

options.content: The Council has never discussed any issue concerning Africa
options.rationale: It has discussed many African issues.

explanation: The veto of the five permanent members can paralyse the Council.
hints: Choose the criticism that relies on the structure of the Council.

stem: Which example best supports the view that the UN has contributed to African decolonisation?

options.content: The signing of the Treaty of Versailles in the Hall of Mirrors in 1919
options.rationale: That predates the UN.

options.content: The 1960 declaration on colonial independence and UN supervision of Namibia
options.rationale: Correct: it shows both principle and action.

options.content: The foundation of the Organisation of African Unity in 1963 in Addis Ababa
options.rationale: That was an African organisation, not the UN.

options.content: The failure of the UN mission to prevent the genocide in Rwanda in 1994
options.rationale: That is a failure, not an example of help with decolonisation.

explanation: The 1960 declaration set a principle for decolonisation, and UNTAG supervised the election that led to Namibian independence in 1990.
hints: Choose the UN action on independence.

stem: Zimbabwe joined the United Nations in 1980.
explanation: Zimbabwe became a UN member in 1980, after independence.

stem: The United Nations has a permanent army of its own that can be sent anywhere without the consent of member states.
explanation: Peacekeepers are supplied by member states; the UN has no standing army.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — an editorial in a fictional newspaper in a small African state, 1966 (invented for this question)

> The Security Council has at last declared that the illegal declaration of independence in Salisbury threatens the peace. Our people watch to see whether the great powers will match their words with action, for sanctions that are not enforced are only paper.

**Source B** — a report by a fictional trade official in a neighbouring country, 1971 (invented for this question)

> Rhodesian exports continue to leave by our railways and ports. Firms in several countries supply goods through third parties, and the cost of the sanctions is borne mainly by those who obey them. Rhodesia's economy has been hurt, but it has not been broken.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What doubts does Source A express about the sanctions?

points.description: Whether the great powers will match their words with action
Sanctions that are not enforced are only paper

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What does Source B say about the effects of the sanctions?

points.description: Trade continues through third parties and neighbouring ports and railways
Rhodesia's economy has been hurt but not broken

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How far do the sources agree about the effectiveness of UN sanctions on Rhodesia?

points.description: Agree that enforcement was weak: A fears sanctions will be paper, B reports trade continuing
Difference: B adds that the economy was hurt although not broken, which is more detailed than A's early doubts
Provenance: A is an editorial written at the start (1966) and B a trade report five years later with detail from experience
Own knowledge: sanctions were evaded through South Africa and Portugal but raised costs and isolated Rhodesia

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The sources agree that enforcement was weak. Source A fears that sanctions will be only paper, and Source B reports that trade continued through third parties. Source B adds that the economy was hurt but not broken, which is more detailed. This is partly because A is a hopeful or anxious editorial written at the start in 1966, while B is a trade report five years later, based on experience. My own knowledge supports both, since sanctions were evaded through South Africa and Portugal but raised costs and isolated Rhodesia.

stem: To what extent has the United Nations been successful in maintaining international peace?

points.description: Aims and powers: Charter, Security Council, collective security, peacekeeping
Successes: no third world war, mediation, peacekeeping (Namibia, Mozambique), sanctions, decolonisation, humanitarian agencies
Failures and limits: veto and Cold War paralysis, no army, Rwanda 1994, dependence on great powers
Comparison with the League; change over time
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The United Nations has been partly successful in maintaining peace. It was designed to be stronger than the League of Nations, with the great powers as members, a Security Council with the power to act and a Charter that bans the use of force. It has not prevented all wars, but it has avoided a third world war, mediated in many disputes, and organised peacekeeping missions in places such as Namibia and Mozambique, while its agencies have helped refugees and children. It also helped decolonisation and imposed sanctions on Rhodesia. But the veto has paralysed the Security Council when permanent members disagreed, especially in the Cold War, the UN has no army of its own, and it failed to prevent the genocide in Rwanda in 1994. I conclude that the UN has been more successful than the League because it has endured and helped to manage conflicts, but it depends on the will of the great powers and has failed in some of the gravest crises.

explanation: Credit aims, successes, failures, comparison with the League and a supported judgement.
hints: Compare the UN's successes with its failures, and compare it with the League.

stem: Assess the importance of the veto in limiting the effectiveness of the Security Council.

points.description: The veto: each permanent member can block any substantive decision
Effect: paralysis when permanent members disagree, especially in the Cold War; protection of allies
Other limits: no army, dependence on members' troops and funds, slow decisions, politics of the elected members
Judgement on how important the veto is

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; balance is attempted and a judgement is reached, but it is only partly supported or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The veto is one of the most important limits on the Security Council, but not the only one. Any permanent member can block a substantive decision, and in the Cold War the United States and the Soviet Union often did so, which paralysed the Council and allowed them to protect their allies. But the Council is also limited by its lack of an army, by its dependence on members for troops and money, and by slow decisions. I conclude that the veto is the most serious structural limit, because it prevents action even when the other members agree, but the lack of resources and political will also limits what the Council can do.

explanation: Credit explained veto, other limits and a judgement.
hints: Compare the veto with other limits on the Council.
